To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dynamic behavior of an instrumented program is very different from that of an uninstrumented program and the dynamic behavior of the instrumentation tool itself can be used to optimize the tool.

(1) The performance of instrumentation tools depends strongly on the dynamic behavior of the instrumented program; (2) The dynamic behavior is highly dependent on the instruction mix of the instrumented code; (3) The performance of a tool can be improved by changing the instruction mix; (4) A simple instruction mix can be achieved by changing the compiler optimization level; (5) The instruction mix of the code can be changed without affecting the performance of the tool by using a JIT compiler

(a) the overhead of instrumentation is dominated by the number of basic blocks executed by the instrumented code, (b) the number of basic block executions is dominated by the size of the program, (c) the overhead of the instrumentation is dominated by its complexity and not by the number of instructions inserted, and (d) the overhead of a JIT-compiled program is dominated by the overhead of the JIT compiler.
